title: Skin and soft-tissue infections: cellulitis, abscess and impetigo (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children with bacterial skin and soft-tissue infections in India: impetigo, folliculitis, boils and carbuncles, abscess, cellulitis and erysipelas, with red flags for sepsis and necrotising infection. Built on the ICMR Bacterial Skin Infections workflow (July 2022); piperacillin-tazobactam dose and renal adjustment from its US label.
findings: Features of each infection, hygiene principles, gram-negative cover in diabetes or immunocompromise, incision and drainage as primary abscess treatment, cellulitis severity and treatment, sepsis red flags, when to suspect methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and every topical, oral, IV and MRSA drug with dose checked against the ICMR Bacterial Skin Infections STW (July 2022).
The STW names vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam for severe cellulitis without a piperacillin-tazobactam dose; the label dose is used.
unverifiedSections: Treatment durations for cellulitis are not given in the ICMR STW; 5–7 days is not stated and is left to clinical response.
The ICMR STW abscess section layout is garbled; small versus large abscess mapping should be checked against the printed STW.
Necrotising fasciitis management beyond red flags and surgical debridement is not detailed in the STW.
Ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily is as printed in the STW; many sources use 2 g once daily for cellulitis — confirm locally.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Bacterial skin infections are mostly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci entering through broken skin. Superficial infections (impetigo, folliculitis) need hygiene and topical treatment; deeper collections (boils, carbuncles, abscesses) need drainage; spreading infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis, erysipelas) needs systemic antibiotics, chosen by severity. Diabetes, immunosuppression, scabies and eczema predispose, and recurrent infection should prompt a search for nasal carriage and diabetes (ICMR STW). Severe pain out of proportion, then numbness, with dark skin suggests necrotising infection needing surgery.
keyMechanisms: Breaks in the skin (trauma, eczema, scabies, tinea) let bacteria in.
Staphylococci form pus-filled follicular infections and abscesses.
Streptococci spread through dermis and lymphatics, causing cellulitis and erysipelas with lymphangitis.
Toxin-producing staphylococci cause blistering and peeling in scalded skin syndrome.

symptoms: Painful, red, warm, swollen skin (cellulitis) (ICMR STW)
Honey-coloured crusts, usually around nose and mouth in children (impetigo) (ICMR STW)
Fever and malaise in moderate or severe infection
physicalSigns: Diffuse tender swelling of a limb (cellulitis) (ICMR STW)
Bright red, raised plaque with a sharp edge (erysipelas) (ICMR STW)
Follicle-centred pustules or nodules (folliculitis, furuncle) (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Temperature over 38°C, white cells over 12,000 or under 4,000/µL, heart rate over 90, respiratory rate over 24 (ICMR STW sepsis signs)
Severe pain then deceptive loss of pain, dark skin discolouration: necrotising infection (ICMR STW)
Bullae, skin sloughing, hypotension or organ dysfunction: severe cellulitis (ICMR STW)
No improvement in 48–72 hours: suspect MRSA (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Oil application, waxing, occlusive dressings (folliculitis) (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Calf swelling without warmth or redness of the skin surface; Doppler.
Pain out of proportion, anaesthetic dark skin, rapid spread (ICMR STW).
Joint-centred swelling and pain on movement.
Tender erythema progressing to generalised peeling; children (ICMR STW).
Itchy rather than painful; no fever.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Typical cellulitis, no pus focus, no systemic signs: outpatient oral antibiotics.
Systemic signs of infection: admit for IV antibiotics.
Failed oral antibiotics, immunocompromise, bullae, skin sloughing, hypotension or organ dysfunction: broad IV cover and surgical debridement.
Incision and drainage is primary; add antibiotics for systemic signs, septic phlebitis, multiple or large abscesses, marked cellulitis or immunocompromise.
Poor immune status, severe systemic signs, MRSA elsewhere, no improvement in 48–72 hours, penetrating trauma.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Desirable; guides change of antibiotic (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: General care
actions: Skin and hand hygiene; no oil on the skin; adequate nutrition (ICMR STW).
Elevate the affected limb in cellulitis; treat predisposing factors such as tinea, scabies or diabetes (ICMR STW).
Analgesia: paracetamol 500 mg or ibuprofen 400 mg as needed (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Impetigo and folliculitis
actions: Oral antibiotic for extensive impetigo, many lesions, lymph node enlargement or outbreaks (ICMR STW).
Ecthyma: oral antibiotic for 7 days, soak and remove crusts, topical antibiotic on the ulcer (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Abscess, furuncle, carbuncle
actions: Incision and drainage or debridement is the primary treatment (ICMR STW).
Add antibiotics only for the indications listed (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Cellulitis by severity
actions: Moderate: admit; IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic (ICMR STW).
Severe: vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam, surgical debridement, adjust to cultures (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Recurrent infection
actions: Look for nasal carriage, diabetes, scabies or eczema (ICMR STW).
Nasal carriers: 2% mupirocin ointment for 5 days a month (ICMR STW).

medicationPlan.note: All doses except piperacillin-tazobactam are from the ICMR Bacterial Skin Infections STW (July 2022). Drain abscesses: antibiotics are adjuncts. Consider gram-negative cover in diabetes or immunocompromise (ICMR STW). Ceftriaxone frequency is as printed in the STW. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Match treatment to infection depth and severity.
Know when to drain and when to add antibiotics.
keyPoints: Mild cellulitis: oral beta-lactam; elevate the limb.
Systemic signs: admit for IV antibiotics.
Pain out of proportion with dark skin: surgery now.
pitfalls: Calling bilateral leg redness cellulitis (often stasis dermatitis).

Return if redness spreads beyond the marked line or fever develops.
lifestyleAndDiet: Treat athlete's foot and scabies in the household.
